newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Tutu slams racism charge against truth probe.
newsitem.headline: Tutu slams racism charge against truth probe.

text.p: Archbishop Desmond Tutu, recovering from a cancer operation, hit back angrily on Wednesday at critics claiming his Truth and Reconciliation Commission is controlled by white liberals.

"The suggestion from anonymous sources in the commission that it is run by a clique of liberals is insulting to me and I take very strong exception," he said in a statement dictated to his aide, John Allen.
Tutu was discharged from hospital on Tuesday after an operation to remove a cancerous prostate gland, but will not know until next week whether his illness could be fatal.

"The implication is that I am almost a token chairperson who is not in control. Anyone who knows me is aware that I am not a person to be manipulated by cliques," he said in the unusually angry statement.
Tutu's reaction followed newspaper reports quoting unidentified black members of the commission alleging that the top jobs were all being given to the minority of white members.
"All major decisions are taken by the full commission.

"Most commissioners are black. Most members of each of the three constituent committess of the TRC are black. The chairpersons of each of the committees, as well as the chief executive officer, are black," he said.

Tutu's year-old commission, appointed to probe the human rights record of South African apartheid and the war against it, has been battered by claims of racism within the organisation and in its handling of inquiries.

The commission said in a statement it would review its inquiry into the white-run media under apartheid following a two-hour meeting on Tuesday with members of the Black Editors' Forum and the Forum of Black Journalists.
"We have to rethink our approach if important stakeholders find it impossible to participate," said Tutu's white deputy Alex Boraine, indicating an apparent boycott threat from the black journalists.

Last year the commission asked the Freedom of Expression Institute (FXI) to prepare a report on media coverage during the apartheid years, when newspapers faced draconian curbs on what they could say.
"The commission is to review the mandate it has given to the FXI in preparations for hearings," the statement said.

The FXI research is directed by Raymond Louw, white former editor of the Rand Daily Mail, which took a vociferous anti-government stance during the apartheid years, before it was closed by its owners, purportedly on financial grounds.
But Thami Mazwai, head of the Black Editors' Forum, said Louw should not be involved in any inquiry because he had been part of a system that discriminated against black journalists.

Mazwai said the Argus Group, now Independent Newspaper Holdings and South African Associated Newspapers, now Times Media Ltd, which dominated press ownership over four decades of apartheid, "hardly raised a sweat in opposition to the then government's stranglehold on the media".
Louw said the objections of black editors to the FXI compiling a report for the truth commission were misplaced because the report would be only one submission among many.
